title: Given a single non-negative integer N, draw a flowchart to calculate and print N factorial (N!), the product of all integers from 1 to N inclusive. Start, read N, initialize result = 1 and i = 1, loop while i <= N doing result = result * i and i = i + 1, print result, End. Special case: 0! = 1, so the loop simply does not execute. Input: 5, Expected Output: 120.
shortTitle: Factorial — print N! as the product of all integers from 1 to N

s1_definition.profdef: The factorial of a non-negative integer N, written N!, is the product of every integer from 1 up to N. By definition 0! equals 1 because the product of no numbers at all is the multiplicative identity, which is one. The standard iterative algorithm keeps a running product starting at one and multiplies it by each integer from one to N, which naturally handles the zero case because the loop body never runs.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India calculating how many different orders N pending cheques can be processed in. The first cheque can go in any of N slots, the next in any of the remaining N minus one slots, and so on down to one. Multiplying those shrinking choices together is exactly a factorial. Rajesh asks how many ways his five cheques can be arranged, and the answer is five times four times three times two times one, which is 120.
s1_definition.oneliner: Factorial is a running product that starts at one and multiplies in every integer from one to N, and because an empty product is one, zero factorial is one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The factorial of a non-negative integer N, written N!, is the product of every integer from 1 up to N. By definition 0! equals 1 because the product of no numbers at all is the multiplicative identity, which is one. The standard iterative algorithm keeps a running product starting at one and multiplies it by each integer from one to N, which naturally handles the zero case because the loop body never runs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India calculating how many different orders N pending cheques can be processed in. The first cheque can go in any of N slots, the next in any of the remaining N minus one slots, and so on down to one. Multiplying those shrinking choices together is exactly a factorial. Rajesh asks how many ways his five cheques can be arranged, and the answer is five times four times three times two times one, which is 120.

**One line to remember:** Factorial is a running product that starts at one and multiplies in every integer from one to N, and because an empty product is one, zero factorial is one.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm needs one accumulator and one counter. You start the accumulator, call it result, at one, because one is the neutral value for multiplication. You then walk a counter i from one to N inclusive, and on each step you do result = result * i. When the loop finishes, result holds N!.

A critical detail for a banking system is overflow. Factorials grow extremely fast, and a Java long overflows past 20!. Because money and counts in banking must never silently wrap into a negative or wrong number, I compute factorials with BigInteger, which has arbitrary precision and never overflows. For example, `BigInteger result = BigInteger.ONE; result = result.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(i));` keeps multiplying safely no matter how large the value gets.

The zero case falls out for free. If N is zero, the loop condition i <= N is one <= zero, which is false immediately, so the body never runs and result stays at its initial value of one. That is exactly the mathematical definition of 0!, so no special branch is needed in the code, though I still validate that N is not negative because factorial is undefined for negative numbers and I reject that with a clear exception.

The time complexity is linear in N because we do one multiplication per step, and the space is constant apart from the size of the big number itself. A senior nuance is that for repeated queries you can cache previously computed factorials, and for very large N you would switch to specialized libraries, but for the arrangement counts a bank actually needs, the simple linear loop with BigInteger is correct and clear.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The operations desk at National Bank of India wants to know, for audit sampling, how many distinct orders a small batch of N cheques could be processed in. The number of orderings of N items is exactly N factorial, so we need a correct factorial routine.

This is exactly how the factorial algorithm works, because arranging N distinct things in a line gives N choices for the first, N minus one for the second, and so on, and that product is N!.

Problem 2 — Factorials explode in size and a plain long silently overflows past twenty, which in a bank would produce a wrong or negative count and a false audit figure. This is exactly why we compute with BigInteger, which never overflows.

Problem 3 — A batch might be empty, meaning zero cheques, and the system must report exactly one ordering, not crash. This is exactly the 0! equals 1 case that the loop handles naturally by never executing.

Our mini-project builds a `FactorialCalculator` service with a `factorial(int n)` method returning BigInteger, validation rejecting negative input, and a `FactorialDemo` runnable that computes the arrangements for Rajesh's batch of five cheques and prints 120.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: N = 5 (Rajesh's batch of five cheques).

Step 1 — The accumulator result is initialized to one and the counter i to one. At this point no multiplication has happened, so result represents the empty product.

Step 2 — The loop checks i <= N, which is 1 <= 5, true. It multiplies result by i, giving 1 times 1 equals 1, then increments i to two.

Step 3 — Next iterations multiply in 2, 3, 4, and 5 in turn. result becomes 2, then 6, then 24, then 120, while i climbs to 6.

Step 4 — The loop checks 6 <= 5, which is false, so the loop stops. The accumulator result holds 120, which is 5!.

Step 5 — For the empty batch, N is zero, so the very first check 1 <= 0 is false, the body never runs, and result stays at one, correctly giving 0! equals 1.

Step 6 — The service returns BigInteger values, so even a large batch would be computed exactly without overflow, and the demo logs both results.

Final output:

```
2026-10-31 23:40:00 [INFO] Rajesh SAV2001: 5 cheques can be processed in 120 distinct orders
2026-10-31 23:40:00 [INFO] Empty batch 0! = 1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: N = 5 cheques
    │
    ▼
  result = 1 (BigInteger), i = 1
    │
    ▼
  loop while i <= N:
    i=1 → result = 1
    i=2 → result = 2
    i=3 → result = 6
    i=4 → result = 24
    i=5 → result = 120
    │ i=6 → 6<=5 false → stop
    ▼
  Output: 120  (empty batch N=0 → loop skipped → 1)
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Factorial Computation ═══

  ┌─ Principles ─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: FactorialCalculator only computes N!      │
  │  Guard clause: reject n < 0 fast              │
  │  BigInteger: arbitrary precision, no overflow │

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │     FactorialCalculator      │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ + factorial(n: int):BigInteger│ throws IllegalArgumentException
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for factorial(n):
    Pre:  n >= 0
    Post: returns product 1..n, returns 1 when n = 0
    Throws: IllegalArgumentException when n < 0

  Call Chain:
  1. factorial(5)
  2.   result = 1
  3.   i=1..5 → result *= i  → 1,2,6,24,120
  4.   return 120
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Factorial of a non-negative integer N is the product of every integer from one up to N, and by definition zero factorial is one because the product of no numbers is the multiplicative identity. The iterative algorithm is simple and reliable: you start a running product at one, then multiply it by each integer from one to N, and when the loop finishes the running product is the answer. The zero case needs no special code, because when N is zero the loop condition fails immediately, the body never runs, and the product stays at its initial value of one, which is exactly the mathematical definition.

The real-world subtlety that matters in a bank is overflow. Factorials grow astonishingly fast, and a Java long overflows past twenty factorial, which would silently produce a wrong or even negative number. In a financial system a silently wrong count is unacceptable, so I compute factorials with BigInteger, which has arbitrary precision and never overflows. I also add a guard clause that rejects negative input with a clear exception, because factorial is simply undefined there.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I used this for an audit-sampling tool where the operations desk needed to know how many distinct orders a small batch of cheques could be processed in, which is exactly the number of arrangements of N items, so N factorial. I wrote a FactorialCalculator with a single factorial method returning a BigInteger, validated the input, and let the loop handle the empty-batch case naturally. When Rajesh submitted five cheques the tool reported one hundred and twenty orderings, and because I used BigInteger it would stay exact even for much larger batches. The lesson I carry from this is that even the simplest arithmetic needs the right numeric type, and in finance that almost always means an overflow-safe type rather than a primitive.
